title: Format String Foothold
description: A single-VM, 32-bit format-string privilege-escalation exercise, following all eight tasks of SEED Labs' Format String Vulnerability Lab against the lab's own server.c.
prerequisites: Comfortable with the Linux command line and basic C (pointers, the stack).
outcomes: Identify, leak through, write through, and exploit a format-string vulnerability to escalate from an unprivileged user to root on the same VM.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# General information

* This game is for educational purposes only.
* The solution of a level is required for later levels.

# Storyline

A single VM runs a format-string-vulnerable UDP daemon as root (`printf(msg)` instead of `printf("%s", msg)`). You log into that same VM as an unprivileged user and attack the daemon over `127.0.0.1:9090/udp` to escalate to root.

This follows all eight tasks of SEED Labs' *Format String Vulnerability Lab* (W. Du) — see ATTRIBUTION.txt.

# Before you start

The daemon never exits (it loops on `recvfrom()` forever) and prints everything to its own stdout, which systemd captures. Watch it live with:

```
sudo journalctl -u server -f
```

Send it packets with `nc -u 127.0.0.1 9090` (or a short Python/`socat` script) from a second terminal on the same VM.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
Access the sandbox, then submit **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview, right-click **`victim`** and click **`Open GUI`**.
2. Login with username **`seed`** and password **`dees`**.

See [documentation](https://docs.platform.cyberrange.cz/user-guide-advanced/sandboxes/sandbox-access/#user-access) for SSH access.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with local sandbox.

levels.title: Recon
levels.content:
Confirm the UDP daemon is running on this VM and find its port.

The flag is the port number.

hints.title: It's UDP, not TCP
hints.content: nmap needs -sU for a UDP scan; ss/netstat show UDP sockets separately from TCP ones.

levels.title: Task 2: Understanding the Stack Layout
levels.content:
Before attacking anything, look at Figure 1 of the handout: it shows where the format string, `myprintf()`'s return address, and your own input buffer sit relative to each other when `printf()` is invoked from inside `myprintf()`.

The flag is: on x86, does the call stack grow toward **higher** or **lower** memory addresses as more functions are called? (answer with one word)
levels.solution: Lower. Each new stack frame is placed at a lower address than the one that called it - which is why, in Figure 1, `buf[1500]` (allocated in `main()`, called first) sits at a *higher* address than `myprintf()`'s frame, which sits higher than `printf()`'s.

hints.title: Look at Figure 1
hints.content: main() is at the top (higher address) and printf() is at the bottom (lower address) of the diagram.

levels.title: Task 3: Crash the Program
levels.content:
Send the daemon several `%s` format specifiers (e.g. via `nc -u 127.0.0.1 9090`). Each one tells `printf()` to dereference the next stack value as a pointer; most aren't valid, and the process segfaults.

Because this program never forks and never exits on its own (section 2.1), a crash takes down the *entire* daemon, not just one request - systemd (`Restart=always`) brings it back after about a second. Watch `sudo journalctl -u server -f` while you send the crash: you'll see the one-time startup line twice - once from before your crash, once from the restart.

The flag is that line.
levels.solution:
```
$ printf '%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s' | nc -u -w1 127.0.0.1 9090
```
Watch the journal: `SERVER-READY` appears once at initial boot, then again a moment after your crash payload, once systemd restarts the service.

hints.title: Why does the whole daemon die?
hints.content: There's no fork() here - one process handles every packet in an infinite loop, so a segfault takes the entire service down.

levels.title: Task 4: Print Out the Server's Memory
levels.content:
**4.A — Stack data.** Send a unique 4-byte marker and enough `%.8x` specifiers to get it echoed back in the output - that tells you how many stack slots sit between the start of the format string and the start of your own input.

**4.B — Heap data.** Using that same offset, place the secret message's address (printed by the daemon at every request... no - see hint) little-endian at the start of your payload, followed by a `%s` at the right position, to leak its contents. Building the binary address bytes by hand in a terminal is awkward - use `build_string.py` in `/home/user/attack-code/` (SEED's own helper script, already on this VM) as a starting point.

See the handout's section 2.4.

The flag is the secret string revealed in 4.B.
levels.solution: See the handout, section 2.4, and build_string.py in /home/user/attack-code/.

hints.title: Finding your offset (4.A)
hints.content: Send a recognizable 4-byte marker followed by several %.8x and count how many it takes to see it echoed back.

hints.title: Where's the secret's address? (4.B)
hints.content: It isn't printed by this program on every request the way earlier labs do - you'll need to find it a different way (e.g. a debugger against your own locally-built copy with the same DUMMY_SIZE, or by leaking enough stack data in 4.A to spot it).

hints.title: Byte order
hints.content: x86 is little-endian when packing an address into your payload.

levels.title: Task 5: Modify the Server's Memory
levels.content:
Use `%n` with the offset from Task 4 to write to a chosen address instead of reading from it - target the `target` variable.

**5.A** — change `target` to any different value, to confirm the write works at all.
**5.B** — change it to exactly `0x500`.
**5.C** — for a target like `0xFF990000`, don't make `printf()` emit that many characters: use `%hn` (2 bytes at a time) and split `target` into its two 16-bit halves, writing each separately. Getting a half down to `0x0000` specifically needs the overflow trick explained in section 2.5 - explain in your own notes why a small target value is the hard case.

The flag is `target`'s value exactly as the program prints it in 5.B (`0x` followed by 8 hex digits, zero-padded) once it reads back as `0x500`.

hints.title: Controlling the byte count (5.B)
hints.content: A width-padded conversion like %.500d lets you set printf's running output-byte-count before the %n.

hints.title: Reaching 0xFF990000 (5.C)
hints.content: Write the low 16 bits and high 16 bits of target separately with two %hn's, each at its own address.

hints.title: Why is a small value hard?
hints.content: You can only ever increase the running output-byte-count, never decrease it - reaching a small target means overflowing all the way around past 2^16.

levels.title: Task 6-7: Inject Code and Get a Root Shell
levels.content:
Combine the read and write primitives from Tasks 4-5 to overwrite `myprintf()`'s saved return address with the address of shellcode placed inside your own input (the stack is executable - `-z execstack`). See the handout's sections 2.6 (shellcode structure, `execve()`) and 2.7 (upgrading a one-shot command into a reverse shell).

`exploit.py` in `/home/user/attack-code/` already has the 32-bit shellcode skeleton from the handout - it's set up to run `/bin/ls -l` as a demo. You'll need to: (1) change the command string to something that gets you the flag, e.g. copying `/root/flag_task3.txt` somewhere you can read as `user`; and (2) work out the actual offsets and addresses for *this* target - the skeleton was written for a different lab (different stack layout, different protocol), so don't expect it to work unmodified.

A full reverse shell (section 2.7: `nc -lvp <port>` on your own session, then a shellcode that connects back to it) is the more convenient route once you've got one-shot command injection working - you can just `cat` the file directly from an interactive root shell instead of crafting a second exploit for the copy step.

The flag is the contents of `/root/flag_task3.txt`.
levels.solution: This exercise doesn't ship a working payload for this target - build and test one yourself, adapting exploit.py's shellcode and the offsets you found in Tasks 4-5. See INSTRUCTOR_NOTES.md.

hints.title: Where does the shellcode go?
hints.content: Anywhere in your own input, at a known offset you can compute an address for.

hints.title: What do you overwrite?
hints.content: The saved return address of the function printf() is running inside - the same one your %n write targets, just a different address.

hints.title: Reading a root-only file as a non-root user
hints.content: Your shellcode runs as root (the daemon's own privilege) - have it copy the file to somewhere world-readable, e.g. /tmp, as part of the command string.

levels.title: Task 8: Fixing the Problem
levels.content:
`gcc` warns about the vulnerable `printf(msg)` call at compile time by default. Build `server.c` and read the warning.

Fix the vulnerability (pass the user's input as a `%s` argument instead of as the format string itself), recompile, and confirm your Task 3 payload no longer crashes the daemon.

The flag is the name of the compiler warning flag gcc reports for this specific mistake (format: `-W...`).
levels.solution: `-Wformat-security`. The fix is to change `printf(msg)` to `printf("%s", msg)` - after that, every `%` character in the input is just a literal character again, and the warning disappears on rebuild.

hints.title: Where's the warning?
hints.content: It appears during compilation, pointing at the printf(msg) line.
